alignment.note: The Vulgate omits the entire father's description of the spirit's destructive behavior (Greek καὶ πολλάκις... ἡμᾶς), instead presenting Jesus's response directly. This represents a major textual divergence where the Vulgate transmits a different pericope segment (Mark 9:23 in standard versification) while Greek and Peshitta preserve Mark 9:22.

Greek employs a coordinated construction with repeated καὶ εἰς linking two prepositional phrases (εἰς τὸ πῦρ... καὶ εἰς ὕδατα); Peshitta uses a single verb ܐܪܡܝܬܗ with two prepositional complements ܒܢܘܪܐ ܘܒܡܝܐ, a more compact Semitic construction. The Vulgate omits this entire clause.

Greek uses plural ὕδατα (waters) with repeated preposition καὶ εἰς; Peshitta uses singular ܘܒܡܝܐ (and in water) with coordinating waw, reflecting typical Syriac preference for singular mass nouns in geographic/elemental contexts. The Vulgate omits this material entirely.

Greek employs a purpose clause with ἵνα + subjunctive ἀπολέσῃ (that it might destroy); Peshitta uses the d- prefix construction ܕܬܘܒܕܝܘܗܝ expressing the same telic function. The Vulgate omits the father's entire plea, presenting instead Jesus's theological response about faith and possibility.
Greek ἀλλ᾽ (but) and Peshitta ܐܠܐ mark the adversative transition from description to petition; the Vulgate omits this transitional marker as it transmits a different verse segment entirely.

Greek presents the father's conditional plea εἴ τι δύνῃ (if you are able [to do] anything); Peshitta mirrors this with ܡܕܡ ܕܡܫܟܚ ܐܢܬ (anything that you are able). The Vulgate, however, transmits Jesus's response Si potes credere (If you are able to believe), reversing the speaker and shifting the conditional from Jesus's power to the father's faith—a substantive theological reorientation reflecting Mark 9:23 rather than 9:22.

Greek uses imperative βοήθησον with dative plural ἡμῖν (help us); Peshitta employs ܥܕܪܝܢܝ with first-person singular suffix (help me), shifting from plural to singular—possibly reflecting the father speaking for himself or a scribal harmonization. The Vulgate omits the petition entirely, continuing Jesus's theological statement.

Greek employs an aorist participle σπλαγχνισθεὶς ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς (having compassion on us) modifying the imperative; Peshitta uses a coordinate imperative ܘܐܬܪܚܡ ܥܠܝ (and have mercy on me), maintaining the singular object. The Vulgate omits this appeal, instead completing Jesus's saying with omnia possibilia sunt credenti (all things are possible to one who believes), a theological maxim absent from the Greek and Peshitta tokens provided.

The Vulgate transmits Jesus autem ait illi: Si potes credere, omnia possibilia sunt credenti (But Jesus said to him: If you are able to believe, all things are possible to one who believes), representing Mark 9:23 in standard versification. This constitutes a major textual divergence: the Vulgate presents Jesus's response while Greek and Peshitta preserve the father's plea from Mark 9:22, indicating either a different verse division tradition or a scribal substitution of one dominical saying for another.
